why_correct: Water exists as ice in its solid state because it has a specific temperature and pressure at which the molecules slow down and come together to form a crystal lattice structure, resulting in a rigid and fixed shape. This is in contrast to other states of matter like liquid water, where molecules are free to move and flow.
easy_explanation: Water exists as ice in its solid state because it has a specific temperature and pressure at which the molecules slow down and come together to form a crystal lattice structure, resulting in a rigid and fixed shape. This is in contrast to other states of matter like liquid water, where molecules are free to move and flow.

why_wrong.B: Water does not exist as ice in its liquid state because it has a specific temperature above 0°C (32°F) at which the molecules start moving faster and break apart into individual molecules. This is known as the melting point of water.
why_wrong.C: Water exists as ice in its solid state because it has a specific pressure below atmospheric pressure at which the molecules slow down and come together to form a crystal lattice structure. This is due to the intermolecular forces between water molecules, such as hydrogen bonding, that hold them together.
why_wrong.D: Water does not exist as ice in its liquid state because it has a specific temperature above 0°C (32°F) at which the molecules start moving faster and break apart into individual molecules. This is known as the melting point of water.

real_world_example: In everyday life, we can see this when we pour water from one container to another - it freezes in its liquid state but then turns back into ice when it reaches a certain temperature.
memory_trick: To remember that water exists as ice in its solid state, you can use the phrase "ice is solid" or "solid ice".
